articles.headline: Browns and Deshaun Watson are doing something that's getting the attention of the NFL
keyFacts: The Cleveland Browns defeated the Baltimore Ravens 13-10 in Week 6 of the NFL season.
NFL analyst Nick Shook noted that the Browns relied on a low-scoring, defensively driven formula to secure the win.
The victory places the Browns alone atop the AFC North division through six weeks of the season.
body: It's wild to think that just a few months ago, the Cleveland Browns fan base was actually booing quarterback Deshaun Watson. Now, they're cheering him on consistently, and frankly, some would make the argument that they owe him an apology.

But the real story here is that the Browns beat the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday in Week 6 of the NFL season, 13-10, delivering another solid statement win that shows they're no flash in the pan. It's the kind of game that simply makes the chemistry between Watson and his offense, as well as the Browns' defense, hard to ignore.
The Cleveland Browns keep finding ways to win after another takedown, this time of the Baltimore Ravens

In a piece about the NFL's Week 6 games, Nick Shook of the NFL's official website notes that in this game, a "familiar formula" produced a win. It wasn't simple or easy, but a win happened for the Browns.

"It's not pretty and it certainly doesn't produce a relaxing afternoon for Browns fans, but Cleveland once again fought through a low-scoring, defensively driven afternoon, found enough offense when needed most, and delivered another game-winning drive," he adds. "Through six weeks, the Browns sit atop the AFC North alone with tiebreakers over the Ravens and Steelers, and a defense that has consistently proven it's going to make every opposing offense's day rather difficult."
So, the Browns made another win happen, and in doing so, they limited the Ravens to just 235 total yards. Baltimore was also six of 16 on third down, which is a testament to the Browns' defense.
"Against a team of Baltimore's caliber, Cleveland's formula withstood its greatest test, an encouraging sign in mid-October," Shook adds. It's hard to disagree with him, either.
The Browns and Watson are getting the attention of the NFL by doing one thing: winning. They just keep winning, and that's what obviously counts in the league.

articles.headline: MrBeast Joins Shark Tank, Invests Quarter Million In AI-Powered ‘Ball 2’
keyFacts: YouTube creator James Stephen Donaldson, known as MrBeast, debuted as an investor on Shark Tank and invested $250,000 for a 55% stake in Ball 2.
Cousins Andrew Brown and Kevin Langdon presented Ball 2, an AI-powered ball filled with sensors that tracks data and connects to a companion app to create new games.
While other investors expressed skepticism regarding consumer interest and marketing, Donaldson and the creators expressed confidence in generating viral appeal.
body: James Stephen Donaldson, the algorithm ruling, product hustling, normal smile having YouTube superstar better known as MrBeast recently made his debut on Shark Tank. During his first episode on the show where celebrity investors put “idea people” through a humiliation ritual, Donaldson cut from the pack to back an AI-powered ball. It rolls. You can throw it. Itâs, yâknow, got AI in there. Donaldson opted to invest a quarter million into the product.

Cousins Andrew Brown and Kevin Langdon presented the Sharks with “Ball 2.” A sequel to ball. Unlike your average foam ball, the second ball is “filled with sensors,” capable of tracking and harvesting data as it is rolled, thrown, bounced and so forth. Reporting information back to a companion app, Brown and Langdon added that through the magic of AI you can instruct the ball to create new games on the fly. Like being thrown further, or being rolled not as far.

For a live demonstration, Donaldson and Lori Greiner competed to see who could shake the ball more. Donaldson won. “It worked way better than I was expecting it to work,” said Donaldson after getting his shake on, “that was cool.”

For the most part, the Sharks seemed characteristically unimpressed by Ball 2. Their primary concern was marketing to consumers. The world is full of balls. There are millions of ball havers. Thousands of ball knowers. And despite disagreements from certain communities, we even live on a giant ball. All balls without AI, and at first glance the ball with AI in it looks no different. Without coming across the video pitch, there would be little motivation to opt-in. “If you put this next to another ball on a shelf itâs a tough sell,” admits Langdon.

While Mr. Wonderful withheld his support, MrBeast was all-in. Donaldson invested $250 thousand for a 55% stake in the company. After a concerned glance at each other, the two cousins turned around and shouted “beast ball!” to the offer. Greiner and O’Leary were skeptical of consumer interest, the latter saying it would live or die on a “viral” moment. Donaldson lives and dies on that same principle, fashioning himself a scholar of YouTube user trends and unironic appreciator of Squid Game (the show and the practice). With a seemingly hypnotic control over nephews and their energy drink consumption, both Donaldson and the Ball 2 crew seemed confident they could get kids interested in their AI play orb.

At just 28 years-old, Donaldson has established a business empire that is as vast as it is dubious. While he boasts about his surgical mastery over social media, he plays it far faster and looser in his other ventures. Whether itâs the quality of his food products, routine allegations over staff treatment or where he decides to open a theme park, his circle of control seems to wane the further you go offline.
As for me, I’m keeping my money in Aurora Castle, the amusement park that’s also a space colony to be built somewhere in Vaughan.

articles.headline: McConaughey urges independents to flex political muscle and vote in midterm elections
keyFacts: Actor Matthew McConaughey urged political independents on Sunday to participate in elections to make them a fair fight.
McConaughey did not endorse either candidate in the Texas Senate race between Republican Ken Paxton and opponent James Talarico.
McConaughey said having three to five independents in Congress would force both major parties to write centrist laws.
body: Actor Matthew McConaughey made a petition to voters on Sunday, calling upon independents to make elections a “fair fight.”
“They’ve been telling us for years that an independent vote is a wasted vote,” McConaughey said. “Well, a great question for our time is: ‘How’s that unwasted vote been working out for you?'”

McConaughey lives in Texas, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton is facing off against opponent James Talarico in a competitive race in the historically red state. The actor, who has appeared in movies such as How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days , Interstellar , and The Wolf of Wall Street, did not endorse either Texas candidate.
“I am here endorsing two things: fairness and reality,” McConaughey said.

Approximately 45% of voters identify as politically independent, according to Gallup , which conducted phone interviews in 2025, sampling more than 13,000 adults, with a margin of error of one percentage point.
McConaughey said independents are the No. 1 political identity nationwide, and yet have been forced to choose between Republicans and Democrats.

“Independent does not mean you’re middle of the road, independent is the original road,” McConaughey said. “Before there was ever a Republican or a Democrat, there was an American. Our birth certificate is not the Declaration of Compromise; it’s the Declaration of Independence.”
DEMOCRATS SEE ‘HOPE’ WITH OBAMA ON CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS HE HELPS BOOST CASH AND ENERGY

The actor said that with such a narrow majority in Congress, it would take only three to five “true independents” to have an impact, since neither party could pass legislation without independents voting with them. Extreme policies on either side wouldn’t pass, forcing Congress to write more centrist laws, he added.
“Nothing passes without them,” McConaughey said. “Every bill has to come through the middle, which means both parties would finally have to compete for the middle.”

articles.headline: Rams kicker Blake Grupe ruled out after suffering knee injury minutes into L.A. debut
keyFacts: Los Angeles Rams kicker Blake Grupe was ruled out of his debut game after suffering a knee injury during the first quarter.
The team announced that Grupe sustained the injury while making a tackle on the kickoff following a 44-yard field goal.
Punter Ethan Evans will serve as the replacement kicker while receiver Jordan Whittington practices holding on the sideline.
body: The Los Angeles Rams' kicking conundrum continues into Week 6, but not in the way you'd expect. After cutting former placekicker Harrison Mevis after Week 5, L.A. seemingly found its solution after signing Blake Grupe to assume the kicking duties. The former Notre Dame kicker made his Rams debut on Sunday and quickly endeared himself to his new squad by netting a 44-yard field goal in the first quarter.

However, things went downhill after that. After initially being listed as doubtful to return, Grupe has been downgraded to out and will not return to Sunday's contest due to a knee injury, the team announced. Grupe suffered the injury while making a tackle on the kickoff following his made field goal. He was seen lowering his shoulder to hit returner Devin Duvernay and came down awkwardly.

With Grupe sidelined, the entire kicking operation is reshuffled. Punter Ethan Evans will serve as the kicker, while receiver Jordan Whittington could be the holder, as ESPN notes he was working on holds along the sideline.

So far, however, the Rams have not called Evans' number to kick. After Matthew Stafford connected with Blake Corum for a 15-yard touchdown in the second quarter, they kept the offense on the field for a two-point attempt, which failed. Then, when they were at the Arizona 27-yard line and faced with a fourth-and-1, Los Angeles went for it, but turned the ball over on downs.

Grupe entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2023, initially signing with the Saints. He played for New Orleans until midway through the 2025 season, when he was released. After that, he made stops with the Colts and Jets before finding his way to the Rams. Coming into this game, Grupe had converted 81.9% of his career field goals (86-of-105) and 98% of his extra points (96-of-98).

The kicking game has been an issue throughout the first half of the season for the Rams, and it came to a head during Monday's overtime loss to the Bills. Mevis failed to convert on either of his field goal attempts, including what would've been a game-winner, which was blocked. That forced Los Angeles' hand to make a change in favor of Grupe, but this latest injury keeps them in a kicking nightmare.

articles.headline: A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
keyFacts: Former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock login with her ICE agent husband.
Using the system, her husband performed 983 searches on 97 license plates mostly registered to Hispanic drivers, WJCL reported.
Six employees were fired after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse, and four of them were later arrested.
body: Now, former Savannah police officer Amber Harpe was fired in August following a department investigation that found she had shared her Flock login information with her husband, Tyler Harpe, an ICE agent. SPD does not share its Flock data with ICE and said sharing access to the system violated the department’s security protocols.
A Savannah police officer gave her Flock login to her ICE agent husband
SPD officer Amber Harpe was fired for sharing her Flock access with her ICE agent husband.

While he had unauthorized access to the system, Tyler Harpe conducted 983 searches related to 97 license plates, which were overwhelmingly registered to Hispanic drivers, according to Savannah’s local ABC affiliate, WJCL. The Harpes defended their actions, saying they didn’t use access for personal reasons and that the searches were strictly for “law-enforcement purposes.”

Interim Major Max Nowinsky originally recommended a light eight-hour suspension for Harpe. However, Major Michelle Halford and Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin disagreed, and they removed her from the force. Harpe was fired, along with five other SPD employees, after an internal investigation uncovered Flock misuse. Four of them were later arrested; however, Harpe was not one of them.

articles.headline: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
keyFacts: US President Donald Trump suspended several Russian sanctions, stating the decision aims to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a historic mistake.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called Trump's suspension an important moment that averted serious damage to the global market.
body: - Published
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment", and saying the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
Trump also claimed in his Truth Social post that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Since then, Zelensky declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing a European Union summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.

Accessories maker ORICO has entered the laptop market with the Obook15, which is now available for preorder in the US and the Philippines.

The Obook15 is a laptop for students, early-career workers and content creators, powered by an AMD Ryzen 7 6800H chip with 8 cores.
A Ryzen 7 chip with room for 4TB of added storage
The processor has 16 threads and a boost clock of up to 4.7GHz, while the Radeon 680M GPU is built into the chip.
Its memory is LPDDR5 running at 6400MT/s in 12GB or 24GB capacity, and the PCIe 3.0 drives hold 256GB, 512GB or 1TB.
The Obook15 comes with two M.2 2280 slots, but the supplied drive occupies one while the other stays empty for upgrades at PCIe 4.0 speed.
ORICO says the second slot supports up to 4TB of added storage, which is four times the capacity of the largest supplied drive.

articles.headline: Ebola: Kenya cases rise to 8, spreads to 8th Congo province
keyFacts: Kenya's Health Ministry confirmed an eighth Ebola case after a 49-year-old man tested positive for the virus.
Congo's Health Ministry reported that the Ebola outbreak spread to an eighth province, recording two cases including one death.
Kenya's health director general said that six patients in quarantine are stable after receiving supportive treatment.
body: Kenya's Health Ministry on Sunday confirmed another case of Ebola, bringing the number of confirmed infections in the country to eight.
News of another patient in the East African state came as health officials in Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported that the outbreak there had spread to an eighth province.
What Kenya's health director general said
"Today, 38 people were tested, and one tested positive for Ebola," Health Ministry Director-General Dr. Patrick Amoth said in an interview on Kenya's Citizen TV.
"He is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker. He developed fever, headache and muscle pain," Amoth said.
He went on to explain that the latest case was a patient attendant who cleaned utensils and linen and had likely been exposed to Kenya's first Ebola case, discovered earlier this month.
Amoth said patients in quarantine were being tested after developing symptoms and that the other six patients were stable after receiving supportive treatment. The first patient died on October 5.
Kenya has been on a heightened state of alert as a major outbreak of the highly contagious disease spread in Congo in central Africa.
Ebola now in 8th province in Congo
Also on Sunday, authorities in DRC said that the Ebola outbreak had spread to an eighth province in the north.
Congo's Health Ministry said that two cases including a death were recorded in Nord-Ubangi province which borders the Central African Republic (CAR).

"We see pockets of Ebola generally going down, but unfortunately geographically it's spreading out," said World Health Organization Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi in an interview with The Associated Press in Beni, eastern Congo, on Friday.
It's currently the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history with authorities recording at least 9,400 cases, including over 4,500 deaths, in the outbreak declared in mid-May.
The current epidemic is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.

Ebola is spread between people by direct contact with bodily fluids. It can cause fever, fatigue, and muscle pain, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Some patients also develop internal or external bleeding.

articles.headline: 63 Years Later, the Stellar Action Comic Strip Most America Never Heard of Deserves Another Shot
keyFacts: The British adventure comic strip Modesty Blaise ran from 1963 to 2001 but was rarely published in the United States due to frequent nude scenes.
Created by Peter O'Donnell, the story follows an orphaned refugee turned criminal mastermind who works as a freelance troubleshooter for British intelligence alongside Willie Garvin.
Titan Books currently publishes the complete series in 27 paperback volumes, offering readers a way to access the classic comic strip.
body: One of the cool things about the internet is how it’s become much easier to find obscure comics from all over the world, such as bandes dessinées, science-fiction serials, and stories buried in old magazine anthologies. For every comic that actually gets translated for release outside its original country, such as Valerian or Yoko Tsuno, there are dozens more that don’t. Many of these are long out of print and kept alive online by small communities of fan translators and preservationists. Finding a good one can feel like striking gold.

This goes double for newspaper comics, which are often viewed as disposable in ways that graphic novels aren't. Surprisingly few of them ever pick up an international audience. Exceptions include Andy Capp and Fred Basset, British strips that have substantially outlived their original creators. They do not include the British Dennis the Menace, which debuted in Beano in 1951, five days after Hank Ketcham started a strip by the same name in America.

The British adventure comic Modesty Blaise, created by the late Peter O'Donnell, was virtually unknown in the United States during its original newspaper run, from May 1963 to Feb. 2001. While it has a dedicated audience to this day in much of the rest of the world, over 25 years after it ceased publication, Modesty Blaise was only intermittently carried in American newspapers. This is usually blamed on its frequent nude scenes, which made it too spicy for American audiences. (Modesty is her name, not her practice.) The one exception for years was the Detroit Free Press, and even it censored a couple of strips.

The few fans that Modesty Blaise had in the U.S. more often came from a line of novels written by O'Donnell, or one of the two film adaptations. 1966's Modesty Blaise, a campy box-office bomb starring Monica Vitti and Terence Stamp, still has a cult following, which led to Quentin Tarantino executive-producing the in-name-only My Name is Modesty in 2004.

If you're too young or too American to have read the original Modesty Blaise strips, they're classics of the format. While not every storyline has aged well, Modesty Blaise is one of the great adventure comics of the 20th century.

I read Modesty Blaise for the first time thanks to the aforementioned online preservationists, but the entire original run of the strip is currently collected in 27 paperback volumes from Titan Books released between 2004 and 2017. While you may have to do some digging to find them all, every volume of Titan’s Modesty Blaise collections, which include commentary from O’Donnell and multiple looks behind the scenes of the strip, is still in print at time of writing. If you like spy movies, crime dramas, or crime shows like Leverage, you ought to check out Modesty Blaise.
Magnets for trouble

Modesty Blaise was "born walking" as an orphaned refugee in the Middle East after World War II, with no knowledge of her birth parents or nationality. She eventually wandered into Tangier, where she assumed control of a local gang and expanded it into an international organization of anti-heroic criminals called the Network. Under Modesty, the Network thought nothing of grand larceny or corporate espionage, but frequently crushed drug dealers or human traffickers that operated in its territories.

After she secured her own fortune, Modesty "acquired" UK citizenship and retired to London alongside her right-hand man Willie Garvin. Both of them are widely traveled and wealthy, with years of training as thieves, spies, and martial artists; Modesty is a crack shot, while Willie is an expert with throwing knives. That makes them irresistible to British intelligence, which often employs them as freelance troubleshooters.

In addition, Modesty's criminal past, unique skills, and knack for danger tend to land her and Willie in trouble, both voluntarily and otherwise. Both of them have that unique pulp-fiction ability, embodied in modern work by Jack Reacher, where either of them can find an old friend or imperiled stranger wherever on Earth that they happen to go. (My personal favorite is in “The Stone Age Caper,” when Willie is lost in the middle of the outback and randomly encounters the one Aboriginal Australian that he knows personally.)

Early on, Modesty Blaise is a Cold War-era pulp action strip to its bones. It’s neatly split into a series of 95 individual storylines, which often pit Modesty and Willie against Communist organizations ("La Machine," "Top Traitor," “The Wicked Gnomes”). Other arcs involve small-time con artists ("The Girl From the Future," "The Moon Man"), crime syndicates ("Death in Slow Motion," "The Maori Contract"), or old rivals ("The Girl in the Iron Mask"). The stakes are often kept low in Modesty Blaise, and that works to its overall benefit. Modesty's usually out for vengeance, justice, or survival, not the fate of the Western world.

Modesty Blaise’s original artist, Jim Holdaway, died suddenly in 1970. Much of the rest of the strip’s run was illustrated by the Spanish artist Enrique Badia Romero (Axa, Judge Dredd). Other contributing artists included John Burns (2000 AD, Heavy Metal), newspaper cartoonist Neville Colvin (who drew a couple of my favorite arcs, such as “The Balloonatic”), and for one and a half storylines in 1979, Private Eye’s Pat Wright.

Holdaway and Romero, the two best-known Modesty Blaise artists, had an incredible knack for economic storytelling. Both could do more with three panels than many later pencilers can pull off with an entire page. It makes Modesty Blaise a genuine thrill to read, as it can fit surprisingly elaborate action scenes within the constraints of an ordinary black-and-white comic strip. Combined with O'Donnell's deft plotting and dialogue, that makes Modesty Blaise one of the best adventure serials of the late 20th century, on or off the comics page. If you’re interested in learning how to draw sequential art, it’s worth studying Holdaway and Romero’s work.

Not all of Modesty Blaise has aged especially well. Sometimes, that's part of the fun of reading it in 2026, such as when some now-obsolete device gets pulled out as a high-tech trump card. For example, in "The Bluebeard Affair" (1972), Willie fools a couple of gunmen with a portable cassette player, which was new on the market at the time. Other stories make a big deal about ham radio, VCRs, Mace spray, or the thermic lance.

On other occasions, Modesty Blaise is simply a product of its time. It was often ahead of the curve on cultural issues like race, with both Modesty and Willie frequently standing against bigots on behalf of marginalized people, but the strip has occasionally proven controversial among modern readers for its use of outdated language. As recently as 2020, a villain's racism towards indigenous Australians in "The Stone Age Caper" (1971) got reprints of Modesty Blaise pulled from a newspaper in Australia.

With those caveats, Modesty Blaise deserves a place on the shelf of anyone who enjoys a good serial adventure. If you grew up in the United States, it's one of the best comics that you might not have never heard of, and Titan Books' most recent collections are a high-quality way to catch up with the series. Check it out.

articles.headline: Israeli filmmakers bring counter ‘NAZA’ programming to Capitol Hill
keyFacts: Israeli filmmakers brought counter programming for a film titled NAZA to Capitol Hill.

articles.headline: What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
keyFacts: Apple launched the Image Playground app to generate customized images and Genmoji using Apple Intelligence.
The app requires compatible Apple devices such as recent iPhones, iPads, or Macs with Apple Intelligence enabled.
A recent update added natural language style descriptions, touch modifications, Contact Posters, and Lock Screen wallpapers.
body: What is Apple's Image Playground app for and how do you use it?
Apple's image generation tool got some noteworthy updates this fall.

Sometimes, a text exchange with a friend calls for a super specific image to express a thought. It's the kind of image that you can't find in the legion of emoji on your phone, or hiding in your photo library — an angry avocado, or a picture of you and that friend on the moon when you've never even been out of the city together. The human experience is complex.

In times like these, you might turn to an AI image generator to meet your needs. For those in the Apple ecosystem, one option is firing up the Image Playground app as a quick way of creating an image that can be customized, saved and even used as a Genmoji in the future. (Genmoji are personalized emoji you can make using Apple Intelligence.)
If you haven't used the app, odds are it's already your phone. Here's a rundown of what Apple's Image Playground is and how to use it.
What is Apple's Image Playground?

Apple initially launched Image Playground in December 2024. The app uses Apple Intelligence to generate images on your device that you can save, share or turn into Genmoji. Image Playground is integrated into several Apple apps, like Messages, Keynote and Freeform, so you don't have to stop what you're doing and open another app separately.

To use Image Playground, you'll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, or an iPhone 16 or later with Apple Intelligence turned on. You can also use it on iPads with an M1 chip or later, or the iPad Mini (A17 Pro), as well as Macs with at least an M1 chip.

The latest version of Image Playground, available with iOS 27, brings a few updates to the app. Perhaps the most notable is that you can now describe what visual style you're looking for with natural language. Earlier versions of the app let you select a few specific (like illustration), but the new "Any Style" option lets you specify "virtually" any visual approach. Other updates include modifying what you've already created with touch and natural language. So, if you ask for an image of a cabin, you can use your finger to select the door, and prompt Playground to change it to red, or even move the selection around. The update also introduces the ability to make Contact Posters and wallpapers for your Lock Screen.
How do you use it?

When you open the app, there are several ways you can go about creating an image. If you're starting from scratch, you can use the prompt box to describe what you want to make. There's also a menu you can expand featuring styles, like animation and sketch. If you select Genmoji from that list, you'll be able to save your creation along with any other stickers you have, and use it as you would an emoji.

There are other ways to start images, too, beyond entering a natural language prompt. Near the prompt box, you can tap the figure of a person, and select a face from one of your photos. For example, if you pick yourself, you can change which photo you want to use as the reference image, and prompt Playground to maybe show you as an astronaut. Below the image, you can enter additional prompts to make changes or use the touch feature to tweak the image.

Similarly, next to the icon of the person, there's a button that lets you use a photo you've taken as the basis for the image. When you're happy with you hath wrought, you can tap the Share button and unleash it on your friends and loved ones.

articles.headline: Alberta independence referendum: Will separatists survive a loss?
keyFacts: Albertans will vote Monday on a referendum asking whether to remain in Canada or start legal processes toward a future independence vote.
Polls indicate four out of five Albertans want to remain in Canada, while Premier Danielle Smith voted against separation.
Separatist organizers said they will continue fighting for Alberta independence even if voters reject the referendum on Monday.
body: Cory Morgan has spent more than 25 years fighting for Canada’s oil-rich province of Alberta to become an independent country. On Monday, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the issue for the very first time. But even if the answer is no, Morgan said he’s in it for the long haul.
“I would respect the will of the voters,” he told Al Jazeera. “If they’ve decided it’s not time to go that route yet, then so be it. But that doesn’t mean I’ll stop.”
Morgan, the founder of the advocacy organisation Pathway to Independence, is among a group of longtime separatists who have managed to push what was once a fringe idea onto the ballot.
Monday’s provincial referendum asks Alberta residents to weigh whether they would like to pursue a binding resolution in the future on the question of independence.

Polls indicate the pro-independence side has little chance of succeeding, with four of five people in the province saying they want Alberta to remain a part of Canada. But Morgan’s focus is on the one in five who don’t.
“That’s not a movement that’s leaving,” he said.
What the referendum will mean for the separatist movement and for Canada as a whole, however, is a more complicated question.
What exactly are Albertans voting on?
Monday’s ballot gives Albertans two options: to remain part of Canada or begin the legal process for holding a future referendum on separation.
A vote in favour of the second option doesn’t mean Alberta immediately becomes an independent country.
Any province that tries to secede would first have to go through complex negotiations with the federal government in Ottawa, other provinces and Indigenous peoples who live in and around Alberta.
Some separatist organisers have been using that distinction to encourage people to vote for the referendum — even if they don’t necessarily want independence.

“Strategic separatists and their leaders have been using that ambiguity, that lower-bar threshold, to entice folks to vote not to leave, but rather to send Ottawa a message that Albertans need to be heard,” said Jared Wesley, a political science professor at the University of Alberta.
He told Al Jazeera that the message may be resonating with some voters.

Data collected by Viewpoint Alberta, a University of Alberta-based research initiative, suggests that two-thirds of voters who support the referendum say they’re doing so for strategic reasons, to send a message to Ottawa.
These are people Morgan calls “reluctant separatists”, people who are “at the end of their rope” and simply want Ottawa to pay attention.
But Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned Albertans against this strategy.

“Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” he told a pro-Canada rally in Calgary on Thursday. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.”
What’s driving Alberta’s separatist movement?

Monday’s referendum has been decades in the making. Separatists have long felt that Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, sends too much money to Ottawa, subsidising the rest of the country while receiving little in return.
They also take issue with federal energy policies that they feel limit the potential of the province’s oil industry.
For Morgan, the resentment stretches back to the 1980s when the National Energy Program was introduced by the government of Pierre Trudeau, former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s father.
The policy used price controls, taxes and ownership rules to keep Canadian energy affordable while directing more of Alberta’s revenues to Ottawa.
It has since become a central symbol of “Western alienation”, a term used to describe the sense of disenfranchisement felt among Canada’s westernmost provinces.
Those tensions resurfaced decades later under Justin Trudeau, whose term began in 2015. His climate policies, including a national carbon tax and a limit on emissions, angered Alberta’s oil sector.
“We’ve been fighting about the same things for 50 years,” said Morgan.
Then came the COVID-19 pandemic. Experts say demonstrations against health restrictions mobilised a new generation of conservative activists, breathing new life into Alberta’s separatist movement.
Trudeau ultimately resigned as Liberal Party leader and prime minister in 2025, amid sinking poll numbers. Carney was elected his replacement.

Last year, under growing pressure from separatist groups, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government made it easier to start referendums, helping bring the question of Alberta’s independence onto the political agenda.

For Wesley, the moment is less about growing public support for independence and more about pressure from within Smith’s governing United Conservative Party, whose members show higher support for separation than Albertans generally.
“We’re having a referendum because Danielle Smith wants us to have a referendum,” Wesley said. “She is looking to solve internal party matters by throwing a question to the broader public.”
Though she called Monday’s referendum, Smith has said she opposes the independence effort, and on October 14, she announced she had voted against seceding.
“In my view, now is not the time to give up hope in our country, not when we have fought so long and come so far,” Smith said in a social media video, explaining her vote.
Could defeat make the movement stronger?
Smith’s political gamble has drawn comparisons with the 2016 Brexit referendum in the United Kingdom, including from Carney.
At the time, then-UK Prime Minister David Cameron called a vote over whether the country should leave the European Union, in hopes of settling a debate dividing his own Conservative Party.
Voters ultimately chose to leave the bloc, triggering years of political unrest.

But Ian Cooper, a political scientist who grew up in Alberta and now lives in Ireland, says a more useful comparison might be a different UK referendum in 1975, when British voters chose overwhelmingly to stay in what was then known as the European Economic Community.
That vote, he said, did little to deter those who wanted the country out.
“The activists who were in favour of Brexit — this is before anybody called it Brexit — they really played the long game,” he said. “It took them 25 years, but they finally achieved it.”
Cooper suspects that, even if Alberta separation is roundly defeated, separatists could take a similar approach, pursuing the issue over the long term to gain prominence and support.
“My impression is that they really are true believers, and it’s really ideologically driven,” he said.
If Monday’s separatist vote fails, Morgan said separatists would need to take a hard look at why they had fallen short and work towards making a stronger case for independence in the future.
He does not believe the underlying grievances can be resolved by working within the Canadian system or by electing a more sympathetic federal government.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged at Thursday’s rally that “the frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real”. He added that Ottawa had made people in the province feel “like our resources weren’t our own”.

The prime minister has tried, amid an ongoing trade war with the United States, to improve relations with Alberta, including through commitments to building a new pipeline to Canada’s west coast and major infrastructure projects.
Morgan admits that, for those whose goal is simply to get more leverage in Ottawa, “it’s pretty clear the movement has been effective”.

“We’ve seen more love from a federal prime minister in the last year than we’ve seen in the last 10,” Morgan said. “The problem though, when it comes to stubborn independence folks like me, is nothing has changed in the system.”
Prime ministers come and go, he added. “We’re just one election away from another hostile one.”
Why the other referendum questions matter
But the referendum could also offer an opportunity to challenge the premise that Alberta’s grievances cannot be addressed within Canada.

The independence question is just one of 10 on Monday’s ballot. Other proposals include restricting temporary residents’ access to healthcare and education, as well as allowing Alberta to choose its own judges.
Smith has encouraged Albertans to vote in favour of the nine other proposals, arguing that they will give her more negotiating power in Ottawa.

“Many Albertans I speak with tell me they want to send Ottawa a message, and I would suggest the best way to do that is to give us a strong mandate on the other nine questions,” she said on social media.

If Albertans back those proposals but Ottawa refuses to make concessions, Cooper, the political scientist, said the movement would have fresh ammunition to argue that meaningful change within the current system is impossible.
“Buried in the nine other questions are the seeds for a future referendum,” Cooper added.
What could keep the movement alive?
Not everyone agrees, however, on whether the separatists can emerge from the vote as a united force.
Wesley explained that people have been drawn to the separatist cause for a variety of reasons.

If there’s a sense that independence is not a realistic prospect, there may be little to keep that group of activists together, he said. They could turn their attention to other conservative issues, such as immigration.
Other experts question whether Alberta’s separatist movement, which is united more by economic grievances than by a shared cultural identity, can endure the way Quebec’s has.
Just two weeks ago, the largely French-speaking province elected the separatist Party Quebecois, which has promised a third referendum on independence after Trump leaves office.
Morgan, however, argues that Alberta does have a distinct culture, shaped by generations of people who have moved to the province in search of prosperity.
“The type of person drawn to do that is often an individualistic type of person,” he said. “They want the opportunity to go out and succeed or fail on their own.”
“And that builds a kind of a distinct culture on its own, even if it’s not a long-built one, as you would see in a distinct area like Quebec with a linguistic difference or in another country.”
Even if Albertans reject separation, he believes the movement has succeeded in forcing Ottawa to take the province’s frustrations more seriously.
“Hopefully some people understand that eventually something has to give,” he said. “So whatever the results are … I do hope, at the very least, they’ve served as a wake-up call to a lot of people.”

articles.headline: Trump says DC golf course ‘restoration’ to start despite judge’s order to pause plans
keyFacts: Donald Trump announced renovation work on a Washington DC golf course will begin November 15 despite a judge's pause order.
Plaintiffs sued to halt the project, claiming it violates environmental laws and alters the character of the historic public park.
Judge Ana Reyes ordered the government to clarify by Sunday evening whether its position changed following Trump's online announcement.
body: Donald Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday that “restoration work will begin” on 15 November to a historic public golf course in Washington DC despite a federal judge’s court order to pause his plans over environmental and historic preservation concerns.

US district judge Ana Reyes had ruled earlier this year that the federal government must give notice before any substantive construction work on the East Potomac golf course could proceed, and last week issued an order halting the removal of trees at the site, which she called “inexcusable”.

Trump said Sunday in a post on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin on 15 November and that it would reopen in about 15 months. He wrote that the facility would be transformed into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”. Trump did not acknowledge the legal fight in his post, which included an artist’s rendering for the course redesign.

The judge in the case took notice of Trump’s online message and ordered the government to notify her by 8pm ET on Sunday whether its position had changed from a court filing Friday that said “at most” Trump has given “preliminary thought” to the rebuilding plan and “there is no final agency action”.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Trump’s announcement on Sunday would conflict with Reyes’s directives.

The renovation is among a number of projects Trump was pursuing to reshape the White House and other Washington landmarks. Many of his projects, including plans for a huge ballroom at the White House, the installation of his own name on the Kennedy Center and construction of a massive arch, have been challenged in courts.

The 106-year-old park and golf course, alone, has been the subject of many emergency hearings as the president has sought to renovate it. While it has been open to Washingtonians of all income levels, opponents of Trump’s plans to turn it into a high-end course have argued it will alter the character of the space and make it less affordable to people.

Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs challenging his renovation plans for the golf course, responded to Trump by saying that the course is part of a national park and recreation facility that is meant for everyone to enjoy. “Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves and we will continue to work with our plaintiffs to defend it from unlawful and harmful intrusion,” Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of the group, said in a statement.

The DC Preservation League brought a lawsuit in February to halt the administration’s takeover of the golf course, alleging that it would violate environmental laws and “irreparably destroy a priceless piece of American history”.
In an 9 October court filing, the Trump administration had asked Reyes to dismiss the litigation, saying it was premature because the “proposed project remains at an early and conceptual stage”.

The following day, however, the government removed about 500 trees from the site, which it said would improve safety at the park and restore its original design, and was part of a 2019 plan that predates Trump’s ambitions for the course. Reyes ordered a halt to the removals.
Reyes has also ordered key members of the Republican administration to testify on the recent tree-cutting and whether those actions are tied to the president’s plans for the historical public links.

On Friday, the government filed a motion to disqualify Reyes and move the case to another district judge, saying her actions had shown “deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy” and “open hostility” toward the Trump administration, according to court records. The plaintiffs in the case oppose the motion.
Reyes was appointed to the federal bench by Joe Biden in 2023.

body: President Donald Trump said on Sunday an initial plan for the overhaul of the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C. has been finalized.

“When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Levels of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said.

Trump has embarked on multiple beautification projects within Washington since signing a March 2025 executive order titled “Making the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful.” Such projects, including building a new ballroom at the White House and refurbishing the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool, have often faced significant legal challenges and have generated headlines regarding Trump’s approach to domestic policy throughout his second term. Trump said the course, which was designed largely by golf course architect Tony Fazio, would open in 15 months and “restoration work” would begin on Nov. 15.
“It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall,” he said of the current course’s condition.

“When the East Potomac Course was originally built, it was famous for no trees, with views of Washington, D.C., for all to see, but now, it is completely overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe.” Trump’s plan faces legal hurdles, as Biden-appointed U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes extended a ban on further tree removal until Oct. 26 early last week. The Trump administration allegedly cut down over 400 trees on the site last Saturday, prompting further legal complications stemming from a lawsuit filed by local preservationists.

The Interior Department maintains Reyes is a “far-Left activist” and the National Park Service was “finally implementing a 7-year-old plan to address tree overgrowth” at the course, citing a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report which found the additional growth of trees shifted the course’s feel away from its original intent. Reyes said last week officials removed the trees “because President Trump demands haste on his redesign.”

The legal tit-for-tat continued on Sunday when Reyes reacted to Trump’s announcement by saying his administration must soon notify the court “whether it continues to take the position” that Trump has “at most… given preliminary thought to” specific plans regarding the course, as it had outlined in a filing on Friday. The Justice Department asked Reyes to recuse herself that same day.

“Judge Reyes’s histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. wrote on Friday. articles.headline: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market
keyFacts: Venture firm Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds this summer, marking only the second time in its history of raising a smaller vehicle.
During an interview at TechCrunch Disrupt, Benchmark partners stated that the firm maintains a consistent pace of only two or three new bets per partner annually.
Benchmark partners explained that their Monday partner meetings continue to have no formal agenda to allow space for being reactive and discussing ongoing market changes.
body: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago, and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle.

But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria.

Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article.
Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark?

Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part.

[As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus.
Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund?

Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight.
Ev, you’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ?

Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn early to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team going out on the field together.

And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer.

Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

Jack Altman: It’s funny. I did the podcast with these guys at the start of this year, and during that podcast, obviously we talked about the commitment to being a small fund, but more than that, what I heard was that they want to be the first people who founders call, they want to be concentrated, and they just care. So much in this industry gets tied up in money and status, and what I felt from the Benchmark team then, and ten times more as I’ve gotten to know them so well, is it’s a group that really cares about founders and helping companies. And I did enjoy being an individual investor. . .but in a market this crazy, I don’t know how I’d feel, figuring it out on my own. Having a group of people who are so smart and focused and driven to learn it with and from has been awesome. There’s no better place to learn.
I’m told you meet on Mondays with no agenda.
Chethan Puttagunta: Jack tried to make an agenda. [Laughs.]
Altman: I’ve got an agenda for next Monday.

Eric Vishria: It’s weirdly arbitrary, honestly. It’s an ongoing conversation. In a time of rapid change, you’re trying to figure out what’s becoming possible that wasn’t possible six months ago, and who’s bending light. We talk about what companies we’re meeting, what piqued our interest and why, what we’re seeing in board meetings. You can try to systematize it, but one of the beauties of five people is you don’t have to. It’s a decades-long conversation that only works if you’re small and actually enjoy spending time together. After this session, we’re having dinner with one of the very few entrepreneurs who has built a multi-hundred-billion-dollar company, someone we’re not invested in, just to stretch our thinking.
Puttagunta: Part of not having an agenda is you need space to be reactive. If a founder needs help landing an executive or a strategic partnership, the five of us can be at their disposal.
You’re an equal partnership. Can one person put the kibosh on a deal?
Puttagunta: Nobody knows. We don’t have rules around it.
Altman: I actually don’t know. I was waiting to see what someone else did.
It’s never happened?

Altman: Because the firm is structured around a low volume of deals, you don’t actually want to have all of this rigor. If we invested in 100 or 200 companies a year, you’d want a CRM and a formal voting process. Because it’s so rare, the lack of structure is a huge asset.

Fenton: One of the differentiating aspects of our brand is we’re not so cocksure to come in and say ‘winner’ or ‘loser.’ It’s not Shark Tank. We sort of feel awe, for lack of a better term, at all the possibilities . . . The occasional case where someone comes in who’s polarizing — the entrepreneurs feel that. If someone in the room doesn’t like you, we’re not a great partner.
Companies are growing faster than ever. I’d think it’s easier to feel you’re missing out on opportunities if you don’t invest with greater frequency. Have you picked up the pace?

Puttagunta: I think the pace is consistent. I think part of the reality of venture capital in our business is that we are not going to be part of every successful company, and that’s okay. There are companies that we identify, we find that the entrepreneur has some great strength, and we want to amplify that strength. And it’s our job to find a way to work with that person. It kind of doesn’t matter how much capital they want to raise, or what structure, or where they are. You just have to work through all that stuff.

One thing that founders are interested in as a trend is VCs backing competing companies. Has that VC-founder pact changed because companies are growing so quickly and expanding into one another’s territory?

Vishria: One of the things we have an ethos around is, we are making a commitment to an entrepreneur, and through that commitment, we’re saying we’re going to work with you in this thing, and whatever that thing is, and we are working closely enough where it matters, and it should matter to them, and as it matters to us. The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly, and so you do have companies that will naturally evolve from one thing to another, or pivot or change, and you are going to get conflicts. That’s just the reality of the of the kind of current dynamic. . .

Of course, we’re maintaining confidentiality and doing those things and fortunate to not end up in in that type of insane direct conflict [as happened recently with rival companies Factory and Cognition]. . . that commitment of exclusivity in that area is really important. But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.

Puttagunta: And I think people are ultra ambitious in this AI era. As the cost of coding new products effectively goes to zero, founders see a surface area and they want to attack the surface area, and so I think it’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other. But there’s a way to be there’s a way to maintain that relationship and be respectful.
Jack, have you made an investment for Benchmark yet, and if so, did you feel a lot of pressure with that first deal?

Altman: I have, a few, and some are recent, so not all are disclosed. My background was software, but since joining, I’ve done chips, robotics and infra. Someone asked me when I joined, ‘How was the onboarding?’ And I was like, ‘It was perfect. There was no onboarding.’ Either Chethan or Eric told me early on, ‘Hey, you’re going to feel tight on your first one. Don’t. You’re going to make many investments while you’re here. This whole game includes crazy power laws. The odds of it being your first are low.’ . . . I trusted they understood what my shape was as a person, as an investor, and I was going to just try to stay as consistent to that as I could.

It really is a group dynamic on a lot of these. The investments I’ve made, I don’t think we would have won them if I didn’t have my partners. I don’t know that I would have been able to know how to get to a yes without them.
Eric, the AI chip company Cerebras was an unusual bet for Benchmark at the time it was made. What persuaded you to move forward with it?

Vishria: We invested in the spring of 2016, in the first round. We hadn’t made a hardware investment in 10 years. The founders seemed good, they had a very simple thesis, and I didn’t understand most of the rest. On the Sunday night before they came back to pitch the partnership, Peter told me it went against everything he’d learned in venture. Then, after the Monday pitch, he had flipped. A big part of it is understanding each other’s instincts. That began a journey of lots of ups and downs and many potential deaths of the company along the way, and it’s far from over. The romanticism of falling in love with a founder and an idea is why we do this.

Fenton: Andrew and his co-founders are heretics. What they were saying was unorthodox, and you see it today, with people dumping on the stock because it’s polarizing. That’s exactly where we have to be as investors. If it’s consensus, why is there a startup?
On that point, Cerebras priced at $185 when it went public earlier this year, jumped to $350, and is back near $185. Why?

Vishria: About six weeks before the IPO, I showed the company stock chart after stock chart: CoreWeave, Datadog, DoorDash, Amazon. Peak to trough, it’s insane how many of them move 500% in a year, up and down. So who knows? You control what you can control, and you update the public markets every 12 weeks. Being a public company takes a stomach of titanium, and the employees have to understand that.

Your former colleague, Bill Gurley, long argued that the traditional IPO process is broken, that that IPO pop benefits bankers and their clients — not the company. He’s a proponent of direct listings. Does anyone here agree with that thinking?

Vishria: I think maybe of this group, I’m the only one who’s worked on a direct listing. It can for sure make sense. I think the reality is for this crop of AI companies, it’s going to be unlikely because they need capital, and they need a lot of capital. At the end of the day, IPOs raise money. Cerebras raised $6 billion. That matters, so I think it’s probably unlikely for this crop just because most of them need capital.
Could a severe correction be coming? A lot of AI companies have exhausted free cash flow. It’s very expensive for companies to borrow. We also just saw the first AI bankruptcy with Character AI.

Randall: Macro is always a fool’s errand to predict with precision. What has changed most since I started investing is the information environment. Character.AI was the leftover corpse of a company whose founder and team were acqui-hired into Google a year and a half ago, and it was already sold for $2.3 billion; its Chapter 11 being read as an AI chill effect shows that the info environment for public equities in tech has been drawn so much into this, like, hyperactive X echo chamber.

If you look at the market today and you see where CoreWeave and Nebius and all these things are trading, those numbers are are due to the ARR figures of two private companies that will probably be public in the next 12 months . . .There’s so much capex and there’s so much investment that runs through the estimated and projected health of OpenAI and Anthropic.

Our companies see so much demand that they can’t get enough compute to serve customers who are willing to pay them at good gross margins. There’s nothing inherently unhealthy about the AI ecosystem. What’s unhealthy is the volatility from data points that are often untrue or exaggerated for clicks. I do think OpenAI and Anthropic going public would be healthy, so the market stops swinging 5% to 10% every time an anonymous account updates an estimate.
Those two companies have also really pulled the center of gravity back to San Francisco. Do you have to be in San Francisco to be a founder now? Are you interested in companies outside of California?

Altman: I don’t know that you have to be here as a founder, but I think it is right now by far the easiest place to get talent, capital, and customers. Probably everyone [on the team] works with companies that are not in San Francisco, but we’re also here in San Francisco every day, so I wouldn’t say you have to, but I’d say: strong bias for our particular setup.

Fenton: Historically, 90%-plus percent of the capital returns have come from companies founded here. There are beautiful stories outside that dense probability distribution — Shopify is a great example, Ramp — but the ecosystem effect that occurs when you have a successful company and that leads to a background of great executives [and] ambitious people, the bar of success gets raised. I don’t think it has systemically happened anywhere quite like here.

Randall: I’m trying to think of a non-SF based company that I’ve met with in the last 18 months that wasn’t actively saying that they were spending time in San Francisco. They’ve either opening an office in San Francisco, they’re spending half of their time in San Francisco, or they’re planning to move out to San Francisco. Iron sharpens iron. If you want to be around peers who are going to make you the best version of yourself, and it’s hard to think of a city that does that better than San Francisco in the current era that we’re in now with AI here.

articles.headline: NFL roundup: Panthers pile pain on slumping Eagles; Williams shines on Bears return
keyFacts: Bryce Young and Chuba Hubbard led the Carolina Panthers to a 25-14 victory over the injury-riddled Philadelphia Eagles.
Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury to help the Chicago Bears defeat the Atlanta Falcons 31-23.
Ka’imi Fairbairn kicked a 49-yard field goal as time expired to give the Houston Texans a 34-31 win against the Jacksonville Jaguars.
body: Carolina Panthers 25–14 Philadelphia Eagles

Bryce Young threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns to Tommy Tremble, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards and a score to lead the Carolina Panthers (3-2) past the injury-riddled Philadelphia Eagles (2-4). The Panthers had little trouble in the second half picking apart the Eagles, who were missing quarterback Jalen Hurts and running back Saquon Barkley. Hurts is on injured reserve and will miss at least four games with a blood clot in his calf. Tanner McKee started for Philadelphia and finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown.
Chicago Bears 31–23 Atlanta Falcons

Caleb Williams completed his first 12 passes in his return from a hamstring injury, D’Andre Swift ran for two touchdowns and the Chicago Bears (4-2) beat the Atlanta Falcons (2-4). The Bears led 31-7 before holding off Atlanta’s comeback attempt in the final quarter. Bears cornerback Kyler Gordon, who returned from a calf injury, had three sacks and two forced fumbles. Gordon’s big day was capped by a sack of Michael Penix Jr and forced fumble with 2:54 remaining and the Bears protecting a 31-23 lead.
Baltimore Ravens 10–13 Cleveland Browns

Deshaun Watson connected with Jerry Jeudy for 33 yards to set up Andre Szmyt’s 37-yard field goal on the final snap, and the Cleveland Browns rallied past the Baltimore Ravens. Cleveland’s first-year coach, Todd Monken, picked up an improbable victory over the Ravens, for whom he spent the previous three seasons as offensive coordinator. Cleveland relied on their defense for long stretches and got just enough playmaking from Watson in the end. The Ravens had Tyler Huntley at quarterback for the second straight week because Lamar Jackson has an ankle injury. Baltimore scored on their first two possessions but did nothing from there. Both teams have 4-2 records.
New York Jets 19–26 New England Patriots

Drake Maye tossed three touchdown passes and the New England Patriots extended their winning streak to three games. Maye completed 18 of 32 passes for 235 yards. Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry had New England’s touchdown receptions, while Douglas caught seven passes for 86 yards. New York’s Geno Smith completed 20 of 30 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown but was intercepted for the first time this season. The Jets (2-4) got four field goals from Jason Sanders and a game-high 11 tackles (six solo) from Jamien Sherwood. Sanders pulled the Jets within 26-19 by kicking a 36-yard field goal with 32 seconds to play, but New England (4-2) recovered the onside kick.
Pittsburgh Steelers 26–19 Tampa Bay Buccaneers (OT)

Aaron Rodgers threw touchdown passes in the fourth quarter and overtime and Chris Boswell made four field goals to lead the Pittsburgh Steelers to a comeback overtime win. The Steelers (4-2) erased a 16-3 fourth quarter deficit with 16 unanswered points in the period. The Bucs (1-5) tied the game at 19 with three seconds left on a 53-yard field goal by Chase McLaughlin. Rodgers led a 12-play, 70-yard drive, capped by a six-yard touchdown pass to Germie Bernard with 3:15 left in overtime. Jalon Daniels, who made his third consecutive start for the injured Baker Mayfield, scrambled 10 yards to Tampa Bay’s own 37 for a first down on fourth- and-nine on the Bucs’ ensuing drive. Five plays later, Daniels was sacked on fourth down by Jalen Ramsey on a corner blitz to end the game.
Houston Texans 34–31 Jacksonville Jaguars

Ka’imi Fairbairn kicked a 49-yard field goal as time expired, CJ Stroud threw three touchdown passes and the Houston Texans beat the Jacksonville Jaguars on the slick grass of Wembley Stadium. Cam Little’s 60-yard field goal had tied the game at 31-31 with just under two minutes left after Travis Hunter intercepted Stroud’s pass in the end zone. Hunter also hauled in a seven-yard touchdown pass at the other end – becoming just the fifth player in the Super Bowl era, including the playoffs, to score a touchdown and intercept a pass in the same game. Marvin Harrison Jr made his debut for the 2-4 Texans as Houston earned back-to-back wins to gain ground on the AFC South-leading Jaguars (4-2).
New Orleans Saints 34–27 New York Giants

Tyler Shough threw three touchdown passes and ran for a score, and the New Orleans Saints (2-4) scored 34 consecutive points, holding on to defeat the New York Giants (3-2-1) and end their three game-losing streak. Isaiah Stalbird forced a fumble on a kick return late in the first half that flipped the momentum in favor of the Saints. Giants fans streamed to the exits after Jameis Winston threw his second interception of the afternoon early in the fourth quarter, and the stands were half-empty by the time JJ McCarthy led multiple scoring drives and fell just short of an improbable comeback.
Tennessee Titans 26–20 Indianapolis Colts

Joey Slye connected on a tie-breaking 49-yard field goal with 2:03 left on Sunday as the visiting Tennessee Titans upset the Indianapolis Colts for their first win of the season. It was the third field goal of the game for Slye, who added a 44-yarder with 43 seconds remaining after Tennessee (1-5) got a fourth-down stop. The comeback from a 13-point halftime deficit gave head coach Robert Saleh his first win with the team. Cam Ward completed 11 of 22 passes for 102 yards with a touchdown and an interception for the Titans. Tennessee notched six sacks, including two apiece by Jeffery Simmons and Jermaine Johnson II. Daniel Jones hit 22 of 42 passes for 269 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions for Indianapolis (2-4) while Jonathan Taylor ran for 94 yards on 21 carries.

articles.headline: Taika Waititi Says His Star Wars Movie Is 'on Ice'
keyFacts: Director Taika Waititi confirmed to Inverse that his long-delayed Star Wars movie is officially on ice.
Waititi stated that he and writer Tony McNamara are currently working on a different project together instead.
Waititi said it remains unclear if his Star Wars movie will eventually happen, adding that ice ages do come to an end.
body: Director Taika Waititi has confirmed his long-in-development Star Wars movie is officially "on ice."

The Thor: Ragnarok and Jojo Rabbit filmmaker provided Inverse with the update when speaking to the outlet during a press junket for his new film, Klara and the Sun . When asked directly for the state of his and writer Tony McNamara's progress in the Star Wars universe, Waititi had a blunt answer.
"I hate to break this to you, but we're going to actually put it on ice and we're working on a different thing together," he said.

Brutal. Rumors that Disney and Lucasfilm had approached the What We Do in the Shadows filmmaker to helm a Star Wars project go as far back as January 2020. That's just a few years after he took off as the mastermind behind one of the most beloved Marvel Cinematic Universe movies to date, with an official announcement confirming he was attached to a movie arriving just a few months later.

It was mostly good news at first. In 2021, Waititi said he had finished his Star Wars movie's story , and in 2022, then-Lucasfilm president Kathleen Kennedy said the goal was to bring it to theaters in late 2023 . At the time, she also admitted that Disney hadn't "locked anything in" quite yet, a fact that only became more apparent in the years that followed.

Waititi was said to be "still working away" on the project on the third anniversary of its announcement in April 2023. After admitting he planned to prioritize other projects later that year, updates went mostly quiet. Waititi finally returned earlier this year to promise that his Star Wars movie was going to "harness a little bit more of the fun from the original trilogy." Now, it's all on ice.

"Well, there's your answer," he continued during his conversation with Inverse. "I don't even know how to dress it up or make it even vague. It's very iced. I've got about four other movies I'm trying to do."

It's years of updates that led to what will no doubt arrive as a disappointing announcement for many, even if it's not too surprising. Going on six years with little more than the occasional minor promise never spelled a bright future for Waititi's Star Wars. When Kennedy said she thought the project was "still somewhat alive" amid her Lucasfilm exit , fans started to expect the worst.

None of this is to say Waititi hasn't stayed busy in the years between. In 2022, he launched Thor: Love and Thunder , with his Next Goal Wins movie then following the next year. Klara and the Sun will bring Jenna Ortega, Amy Adams, Steve Buscemi, and the rest of its all-star cast to theaters October 23, 2026, even if negative reviews have cast shade on its premiere. Early reception has landed it with a painful 23% on Rotten Tomatoes after 12 reviews so far.
For now, it's unclear if his Star Wars movie will ever come to be. Even he sounded a bit unsure of what the future holds, adding, "Ice ages do come to an end. Who knows?"
